content: Blood transfusions are associated with significant risks, including morbidity and mortality. To mitigate these risks, the prophylactic use of loop diuretics—such as furosemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid, or torsemide—is a common practice, particularly in patients at risk of circulatory overload, pulmonary edema, or both. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the prophylactic administration of loop diuretics provides a therapeutic benefit, specifically a favorable risk-benefit ratio, in adults and children receiving any type of blood product transfusion. This was compared to placebo, no treatment, or general fluid restriction strategies. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed in the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register up to January 13, 2015. The search was facilitated by the Trials' Search Coordinator and utilized terms relevant to the topic. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that assessed the use of loop diuretics in patients undergoing blood transfusion. Two independent reviewers evaluated the quality of the studies and extracted data. When necessary, study authors were contacted for additional information. The results were intended to be expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) with 95% CI for continuous outcomes. Random-effects models were planned for calculating mean effect sizes. The review included four studies involving a total of 100 participants. Furosemide was the only loop diuretic investigated across all four studies. However, none of the included studies assessed the clinically significant outcomes specified in the review protocol. Instead, the studies focused on various markers of respiratory function. One study reported an improvement in the fraction of inspired oxygen (favoring furosemide), while two studies noted an improvement in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (also favoring furosemide). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether the prophylactic administration of loop diuretics in patients undergoing blood transfusion effectively prevents clinically significant transfusion-related morbidity. Despite the widespread use of loop diuretics in this context, this review underscores the lack of evidence to support the practice. Therefore, well-designed randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to evaluate the therapeutic utility of pre-transfusion loop diuresis. This is particularly critical given the high mortality, severe morbidity, and increasing incidence of transfusion-associated circulatory overload.
